title: Building a Query Planner: Testing Strategy to Validate Correctness in SpiceDB
summary: For a permissions database, a wrong answer is a security bug. See how consistency, property-based, and steelthread tests validate the SpiceDB Query Planner.
body_markdown:
This post is part 3 of our series on the SpiceDB Query Planner. Read[part 1](https://authzed.com/blog/introducing-spicedb-query-planner) and[part 2](https://authzed.com/blog/query-planner-early-benchmarks) .


In our[previous blog post about Query Planner](https://authzed.com/blog/introducing-spicedb-query-planner) , we laid out a vision for how a modern query planner could improve the performance of a relationship-based access control database like SpiceDB. Query planners are traditionally found in relational databases like Postgres, where they improve the performance of queries such as SELECT by splitting execution into two stages (planning and execution) rather than executing everything in a single step.


This post continues our series on developing the experimental Query Planner in SpiceDB, providing a deep dive into its design and implementation. Today, we cover recent developments in the first phase of work: **correctness** .


For a permissions database, correctness is the top priority. If SpiceDB returns the **wrong** answer to a Check request, it doesn't matter how fast it responded; any incorrect answer is, at minimum, a security vulnerability. This sets SpiceDB apart from traditional databases. If Postgres returns an incomplete set of rows for a query, it is certainly a bug, but whether it becomes a security issue depends on the **context** of the application rather than being an inherent breach.


One of our primary goals in developing the Query Planner has been identifying and resolving correctness issues early, before the experimental planner ever touches a production environment. To achieve this, we rely on four testing strategies in SpiceDB: unit tests, consistency tests, property-based tests, and steelthread tests. Since unit tests are standard, we'll first start by looking at SpiceDB's consistency test suite.


## Consistency Tests


In SpiceDB, a "consistency test" verifies that for a **specific** schema and set of pre-defined relationships, all API responses remain consistent with one another. For instance, if a CheckPermission request returns` PERMISSIONSHIP_HAS_PERMISSION` , the resource-and-subject pair **must** also appear in the output of` LookupResources` and` LookupSubjects` (and vice versa). If they differ, the API implementations are out of sync, signaling a bug in one or more endpoints.


Consistency tests are implemented in[consistency_test.go](https://github.com/authzed/spicedb/blob/main/internal/services/integrationtesting/consistency_test.go) , which loads configurations from the[testconfigs](https://github.com/authzed/spicedb/tree/main/internal/services/integrationtesting/testconfigs) directory. Each YAML file in that directory represents a single consistency test, specifying the schema, relationships, and expected assertions. Notably, this uses the **exact** format used by the[SpiceDB Playground](https://play.authzed.com/) , making test cases fully interchangeable between the two.


Consistency tests execute in a number of steps:


First, the test runner constructs a SpiceDB datastore (using an in-memory store by default, though a subset runs against production datastore backends). It writes the schema with full validation, applies each relationship via the WriteRelationships API, and reads them back. This verifies that schema writes and relationship updates work as expected across all input scenarios.


Second, the predefined assertions are executed as CheckPermission calls to validate the baseline state intended by the test author.


Third, the test constructs an "accessibility set," representing every accessible subject across all resource and permission combinations. For example, in a schema with a` view` permission on a` document` , the accessibility set collects every user who has access to **each** document by running` CheckPermission` across every subject and resource pair.


Finally, the runner calls LookupResources, LookupSubjects, ExpandPermissionTree, and several other APIs against **every combination** of resource, permission, and subject, cross-checking the results across APIs to ensure full consistency.


To support the Query Planner, we integrated it as another consumer of the consistency test suite in[query_plan_consistency_test.go](https://github.com/authzed/spicedb/blob/main/internal/services/integrationtesting/queryconsistency/query_plan_consistency_test.go) . This ensures that the Query Planner's output matches the legacy implementation across all existing APIs.


Consistency tests quickly proved their worth by uncovering numerous bugs during early Query Planner development. However, they have a fundamental blind spot: they only test *known* schema structures and relationships. If an edge case isn't covered by a predefined scenario, the bug will remain hidden until encountered in production.


To **proactively** catch these unknown edge cases, we introduced **property-based testing** .


## Property-Based Tests


Property-based testing takes a proactive approach to validation. Instead of testing static scenarios, a property-based test defines a set of **properties** , such as the valid structural shapes (definitions and permissions operations) allowed within a schema. The testing framework continuously generates randomized test cases based on these rules, starting from a random seed. This allows us to explore a vastly larger state space without manually authoring every permutation.


When a property-based test discovers a failure, the framework automatically shrinks the failing input down to a minimal reproducible test case, which can then be saved as a standard test for regression tracking and TDD fix development.


In SpiceDB, property-based testing began with the[v2 schema package](https://github.com/authzed/spicedb/tree/main/pkg/schema/v2) , which was designed from the ground up to compose modular schema components. Built on top of this, the[testing package](https://github.com/authzed/spicedb/tree/main/pkg/schema/v2/testing) leverages[rapid](https://pgregory.net/rapid) , a Go property-based testing framework, to generate randomized schemas and corresponding relationship tuples.

While generated schemas are dense and synthetically named, these scenarios are automatically fed into both the Query Planner integration tests and the consistency testing suite for exhaustive verification.


Property-based testing has already uncovered subtle logical edge cases. When a bug is found, we often simplify the generated case and add it to our permanent consistency test suite for explicit coverage. Combined with unit and consistency tests, property-based testing has significantly raised our confidence in correctness.


Unit, consistency, and property-based tests still share one common limitation: they evaluate component logic in isolation rather than testing complete API calls end-to-end.


## Steelthread Tests


To bridge this gap, SpiceDB relies on "steelthread tests."


Named after the[software architecture concept](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steel_thread) , itself originally based on a bridge building technique (yes, really!), steelthread tests execute end-to-end requests with predefined inputs and outputs through every layer of the SpiceDB stack.


In SpiceDB,[steelthread operations](https://github.com/authzed/spicedb/blob/c311f7a768711fe3183921241874d48ca09eae60/internal/services/steelthreadtesting/definitions.go#L71) execute complete API requests through request validation, caching, concurrency controls, core permission logic, and datastore backends. This lets us validate proof-of-concept changes in the Query Planner, ensure full stack compatibility, and verify that complex or unusual queries behave consistently and performantly across both legacy and new execution paths.


## Summing Everything Up


Correctness is paramount for a permissions database like SpiceDB, and ensuring that Query Planner produces the right results is a critical first step toward making it production-ready. By combining consistency tests, property-based tests, and steelthread tests, alongside our existing unit tests, we've built a layered approach to identifying correctness issues early and across a wide variety of scenarios.


Consistency tests ensure that Query Planner agrees with the existing SpiceDB implementations, property-based tests help uncover edge cases that we might never have thought to test manually, and steelthread tests verify that everything continues to work correctly through the entire SpiceDB stack. Together, these approaches have already helped us identify and resolve numerous issues, giving us significantly greater confidence in the correctness of Query Planner as we continue its development. While there's still more work ahead, this testing foundation puts us in a much stronger position to move forward with the next phases of the project.
